title: Task-Optimized Convolutional Recurrent Networks Align with Tactile Processing in the Rodent Brain
paper_category: Computational Neuroscience / NeuroAI (task-optimized deep network models of sensory cortex, NeurIPS 2025)

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A4 'Inter-Animal Consistency': 'We found the mean pooled animal score was 0.175 with a s.e.m. of 0.161 and maximum score of 1.34.'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A noise-corrected RSA Pearson's r (a correlation) is bounded on [-1, 1], so a maximum of 1.34 is mathematically impossible. The main text (Fig. 4b caption) reports 'the maximum between all pairs of animals is 0.34' and the in-figure annotation reads '0.34 inter-animal max'. The means agree to rounding (0.175 vs 0.18), confirming the two passages report the same statistic; the maxima (1.34 vs 0.34) are internally contradictory, and 1.34 also lies ~7.2 s.e.m. above the reported mean, implausible for a bounded statistic. This is load-bearing because the inter-animal ceiling is the benchmark the paper claims to surpass.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A1, Table 1, row (1): 'Total Sweeps' = 316,192; caption: 'The total number of sweeps equals the number of sweep augmentation combinations × 9981 objects'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Row (1) lists Speed {30 mm/s} × Height {-5, 0 mm} × Rotation {0, 30, 90, 120°} × Distance {5, 8 mm} × Size {40 mm} = 1×2×4×2×1 = 16 combinations. Under the caption's stated rule this gives 16 × 9981 = 159,696, not 316,192. Moreover 316,192 / 9981 = 31.68, which is not an integer, so no integer combination count can reproduce the printed total (31×9981 = 309,411; 32×9981 = 319,392). Row (2) divides exactly (2,076,048 / 9981 = 208), confirming the rule is intended literally. The reported size of the Low-Variation/High-Fidelity dataset is therefore arithmetically impossible as printed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph 1: 'specialized insect hairs respond to wind stimuli, providing information essential for flight stability and agility [Sterbing-D'Angelo et al., 2011]'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The cited reference (listed in the paper's own bibliography) is Sterbing-D'Angelo et al., PNAS 108(27):11291-11296, 2011, titled 'Bat wing sensors support flight control' (DOI 10.1073/pnas.1018740108). Web verification confirms it studies stiff domed hairs on the BAT wing membrane (mammals) that respond to airflow for stall detection — not 'specialized insect hairs'. The claim as written is therefore not supported by the cited work; the sentence misattributes a bat study to insect mechanosensation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A4, 'Spearman-Brown Correction' display equation: 'RSA~(X, Y) := Corr(RDM(x), RDM(y)) = 2 RSA(X, Y) / (1 + RSA(X, Y))'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: As printed the equation defines RSA~(X,Y) as Corr(RDM(x),RDM(y)) and simultaneously as the Spearman-Brown-corrected value 2·RSA(X,Y)/(1+RSA(X,Y)), while RSA(X,Y) is used elsewhere (Eq. 11 numerator) with the same meaning Corr(RDM(x),RDM(y)). Taken literally the identity collapses to r = 2r/(1+r), which holds only at r = 0 or r = 1. The raw definition belongs on RSA(X,Y), and the tilde quantity should be defined purely as the corrected value; as written the definition is circular. This quantity is the denominator of Eq. 11, so the error propagates into every noise-corrected neural-fit score.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 3 caption: 'Models with the encoder being S4 are excluded as the training losses explode before the first epoch is finished' vs. Results ('ConvRNN encoders ... generally outperformed the purely feedforward ResNet18 and SSM (S4) encoders in supervised tactile categorization tasks (Fig. 3)'), Abstract ('superior encoders to purely feedforward and state-space architectures') and Discussion ('superior in tactile categorization performance ... compared to feedforward (ResNet) and state-space models (SSM)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: One of the two headline claims is that ConvRNN encoders outperform state-space (S4) encoders on categorization, but the figure cited for that claim (Fig. 3) explicitly excludes S4 because training diverged before the first epoch. An architecture that cannot be trained to any categorization result cannot serve as a demonstrated comparison point; the claim that ConvRNNs beat S4 'in tactile categorization' is therefore not supported by the results actually presented.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods ('Applying traditional image augmentations like color jitter or grayscale causes the models to fail to train') and Figure 5c caption ('The models could not be trained with image augmentations') vs. Results ('showed better convergence compared to those trained with standard image-based augmentations ... which were less effective under tested conditions') and the plotted 'image aug.' rows in Fig. 5c
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Models that 'fail to train' or 'could not be trained' cannot simultaneously be a scored comparison condition with reported values plotted in Fig. 5c. The Results hedge ('less effective under tested conditions') directly contradicts the categorical 'fail to train' statements elsewhere. The paper gives three incompatible accounts of the image-augmentation baseline.

predicted_errors.error_location: References: 'R. A. Grant. Can we study whisker movements to gain insights into the natural sensory behaviours of mammals? The Journal of Physiology, 2025.'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A full-text scan finds the string 'Grant' only inside the reference list; the citation key is never invoked in the Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, or Appendix, so this is a dangling, uncited bibliography entry. Web verification confirms the reference itself is real (J. Physiol. 603(22):6733-6745, DOI 10.1113/JP288053, PMID 40504876), so this is not a fabricated citation but a leftover uncited entry that should be either cited or removed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A1, Table 1, row (2): 'Total Sweeps' = 2,076,048; caption: 'For dataset (2), the speed, rotation, and size are each sampled from the range 26 times'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 2,076,048 / 9981 = 208 exactly, so the implied number of augmentation combinations is 208. But the caption's description (speed, rotation, and size each sampled 26 times; height {-3, 0, 3} = 3 values; distance {5} = 1) yields either 26×26×26×3 = 52,728 combinations, or under a joint-sampling reading 26×3 = 78 — neither equals 208. The tabulated total is inconsistent with the described sampling scheme under any literal reading.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 5 caption (a): 'The task performance of SSL models is about one order of magnitude below the performance of supervised models'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Top-5 accuracy is bounded on [0,1]. Appendix Table 7 reports SSL top-5 accuracies of 0.15 (Inter+SimCLR) and 0.23 (Resnet+Mamba+SimCLR), while supervised models reach roughly 0.5-0.6 (Fig. 3). That is a factor of ~3-4, not 'one order of magnitude' (a factor of 10). The claim overstates the supervised-vs-SSL performance gap.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure A1(a) legend: 'Attender: cnn, gpt, llama, none / Encoder: vanilla, resnet, ugmn, inter, whisking / Loss: supervised, simclr, simsiam, vicreg'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The legend categories 'llama', 'cnn', 'whisking', and 'vicreg' appear nowhere in the Methods, Results, or Tables 3-5; the declared search space is Zhuang/ResNet/S4 encoders, Transformer (GPT)/Mamba/None attenders, and SimCLR/SimSiam/AE/supervised losses. The legend is stale (reused from an earlier figure script) and mislabels the plotted models, including a VICReg loss and a 'whisking' encoder that are never described.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods 'Neural Data Comparison': 'binned into intervals of approximately 45-50 ms, corresponding neatly with the 15-20 Hz whisking frequency typical of rodents (50 ms per cycle at 20 Hz)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Period = 1/frequency. The parenthetical is correct (20 Hz → 50 ms), but a 45-50 ms bin corresponds to 20-22 Hz, not the claimed 15-20 Hz band. The 15 Hz end of the claimed range has a period of 1/15 ≈ 66.7 ms, which does not match a 45-50 ms bin. The stated 'neat correspondence' with 15-20 Hz is arithmetically wrong; the bins actually match only the 20 Hz end.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results ('the best models saturated all of the held-out explainable neural variance ... thereby robustly passing the NeuroAI Turing Test on this dataset') vs. Discussion/Limitations ('enabling models to approach and potentially surpass this theoretical ceiling of neural predictivity') vs. Abstract ('closely approximate neural representations in rodent somatosensory cortex under specific conditions, showing a moderate correlation ... albeit with limitations imposed by dataset size and stimulus variability')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Results assert the explainable-variance ceiling has already been fully saturated and the inter-animal benchmark already surpassed; the Limitations say models may 'approach and potentially surpass' the ceiling only in the future (implying it has not yet been reached); and the Abstract describes only a 'moderate correlation' under specific conditions. The three sections give materially different accounts of whether the ceiling was saturated, with the Results claim substantially stronger than the hedged Abstract and Limitations.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 5b in-plot annotation 'r = 0.60' vs. Figure 5 caption ('we find the correlation r = 0.59') and Results body ('a linear trend between tactile supervised categorization performance and neural fit (r = 0.59, Fig. 5b)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The same best-fit correlation between supervised categorization performance and neural fit is annotated in the panel as r = 0.60 but reported as r = 0.59 in both the figure caption and the body text. The two values disagree in the third significant digit of a headline statistic; one of them must be corrected.

summary: Exhaustive-mode verification (strictness=lenient) of the NeurIPS 2025 submission 'Task-Optimized Convolutional Recurrent Networks Align with Tactile Processing in the Rodent Brain' (45 snippets: 17 text sections, 13 equations, 8 figures, 7 tables). All snippets were routed to specialist verifiers (text, math, statistical, vision, citation) plus a whole-paper cross-section consistency pass. 13 findings survived; three are high-confidence (>= 0.85). The most serious problems: (1) Appendix A4 reports a 'maximum score of 1.34' for the inter-animal consistency ceiling, which is mathematically impossible for a correlation (bounded in [-1,1]) and directly contradicts the 0.34 maximum given in Fig. 4b and the main text; (2) Table 1 row (1) reports 316,192 total sweeps, which is not a multiple of the stated 9981 objects and does not match its own 16-combination augmentation grid (16 x 9981 = 159,696), and row (2)'s implied 208 combinations are also inconsistent with the described sampling; (3) a citation attributes bat wind-sensing research (Sterbing-D'Angelo et al., 2011, 'Bat wing sensors support flight control') to 'specialized insect hairs'. Secondary issues include a circular as-printed Spearman-Brown correction (the denominator of Eq. 11, underlying every neural-fit score), a claim that ConvRNNs outperform S4 encoders while the figure showing this excludes S4 entirely, contradictory accounts of the image-augmentation baselines ('fail to train' yet plotted as scored conditions), a dangling uncited Grant (2025) bibliography entry (verified real but never cited in the body), a 'one order of magnitude' performance-gap overstatement, a stale Figure A1 legend (llama/vicreg/'whisking' never used in the experiments), an arithmetic mismatch between 45-50 ms neural bins and the claimed 15-20 Hz whisking band, a cross-section tension over whether the explainable-variance ceiling was saturated, and a headline r = 0.60 vs r = 0.59 discrepancy. The findings read as bookkeeping/arithmetic errors, stale figure legends, misattributions, and overstatement relative to the presented data rather than fabrication. Given three high-confidence errors, the paper requires correction.
